nameStory: The flying gurnard gets its dramatic name from its enormous, wing-like pectoral fins that can spread wide like a bird's wings. When threatened or excited, this fish fans out these spectacular fins, creating the illusion that it might actually take flight through the water. It's also called the helmet gurnard because of its large, armored head that resembles a warrior's protective headgear.
description: The flying gurnard is one of New England's most unusual and spectacular fish, looking like something from a fantasy novel. This bottom-dwelling fish has massive, colorful pectoral fins that can spread like wings, along with a heavily armored head and body covered in bony plates. When fully grown, they can reach impressive sizes and are unmistakable when their wing-like fins are displayed. These tropical visitors occasionally venture into New England's warmer waters during summer months.

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Enormous pectoral fins that spread like colorful wings, often with beautiful blue spots and intricate patterns that feel firm and leathery to the touch

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Heavily armored, box-like head and body covered in hard, bony plates that feel rough and rigid like sandpaper

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Mottled browns and tans on the body with striking blues, greens, and iridescent spots on the wing-like fins that shimmer in the light

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small mouth positioned underneath the large, blunt head, adapted for picking food off the bottom

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found on sandy or muddy bottoms in deeper coastal waters, often partially buried with only the eyes and top of head visible

habitat: In New England waters, flying gurnards are rare visitors found in deeper coastal areas with sandy or muddy bottoms, typically in waters warmer than our usual temperatures. They prefer depths where they can rest on the bottom and blend in with the sediment. These fish are most likely encountered in offshore waters during the warmest months when Gulf Stream currents bring tropical species northward.

seasonality.spring: Very rarely seen as waters are still too cold for these tropical visitors to venture this far north.
seasonality.summer: Most likely time to encounter flying gurnards in New England waters when warm currents bring them northward from their tropical homes.
seasonality.fall: Occasional sightings possible in early fall if warm water conditions persist, but they'll retreat south as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters, having returned to warmer southern waters or deeper offshore areas.

funFact: Despite their name and wing-like fins, flying gurnards cannot actually fly or glide above water like flying fish do - instead, they use their spectacular fins for underwater "flying," gliding gracefully along the seafloor and startling predators with their sudden, dramatic fin displays.
confusionNotes: The wing-like pectoral fins make flying gurnards virtually impossible to confuse with any other New England fish when displayed, but when the fins are folded, the armored body might be mistaken for a sculpin or sea robin - however, no other local fish has the combination of bony armor plating and such enormous, colorful pectoral fins.
contextualKnowledge: Flying gurnards are not true gurnards despite their name - they belong to their own distinct family and are more closely related to seahorses and pipefish than to the sea robins that are sometimes called gurnards in New England waters.
compareHints: As the only species in its genus Dactylopterus, the flying gurnard is unique in New England waters. Its closest relatives are found in the Indian and Pacific Oceans, making any flying gurnard spotted in New England waters definitely this species. No other fish in our region combines the massive, wing-like pectoral fins with the heavily armored body that characterizes this remarkable family.
